newsitem.title: ITALY: Canada may lead Zaire force, Boutros optimistic.
newsitem.headline: Canada may lead Zaire force, Boutros optimistic.

text.p: U.N. Secretary General Boutros Boutros-Ghali said on Tuesday Canada was ready to lead a multinational force in Zaire and expressed optimism that progress was being made to end an "intolerable" tragedy.

Boutros-Ghali told a news conference in Rome, where he is attending a world food summit, that he expected more than 12 countries would make up the Canadian-led force and hoped that the United States would provide logistical support.
"I hope in the next few days we will be able to have these multinational forces and we will have a mandate from the Security Council," Boutros-Ghali said.

The U.N. chief said he had been in contact with Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien on Monday and welcomed Canada's leading role in efforts to bring vital relief to more than a million Hutu refugees displaced by four weeks of fighting.
"I express my gratitude to Canada. Canada has accepted to command these multinational forces...Canada is a very neutral country," he said.
"I am optimistic...the situation is markedly better than it was a week ago," he added.

Boutros-Ghali said South African President Nelson Mandela and some European states including Italy had agreed in principle to commit troops to the humanitarian force to help the victims of fighting between the Zairean army and Tutsi-led rebels.

"We are in contact with Canada, Italy, France, Spain and we hope also to have logistical support from the United States," he said. The size of the force had not yet been decided but he added: "People are talking of between 10,000 and 12,000 with the cost shared by member states who are participating."

France has pushed for troops to be sent to Zaire to open humanitarian corridors to get food and water to starving Rwandan and Burundian refugees and displaced Zaireans, and has blasted the United States and other nations for dragging their feet.

In Paris, Foreign Minister Herve de Charette told parliament: "I hope we will have the answers we are waiting for in the coming hours so that the Security Council will finally be able to meet and take the necessary decision."
Spanish Foreign Minister Abel Matutes said the United Nations might give a green light within 48 hours to the deployment of a multinational force in Zaire.

Boutros-Ghali said he was confident a Canadian-led force, with African participation, would prove acceptable to Rwanda's Tutsi-led government, which has refused to agree to leadership from Paris. It says French troops sent in 1994 to help end genocide protected Hutus blamed for the slaughter.

"I believe that the fact the force is under Canadian command and the fact that we will have more than 12 different nations is a proof that this force is a real multinational force and is a real neutral force," he said, in answer to a question.
"We cannot tolerate people dying due to starvation."
Boutros-Ghali said he met Catherine Bertini, executive director of the U.N.'s World Food Programme, on Monday. "We are thinking of airdropping food...we are discussing this," he said.
Aid workers in rebel-held Goma in eastern Zaire on Tuesday reported delays in distributing food and medicine because of long talks between aid agency officials and rebel leaders.
Asked whether his efforts to speed up action on the Zairean tragedy would boost his hopes of being re-elected as secretary-general despite U.S. opposition, Boutros-Ghali said:

"I have to finish my job and do whatever must be done to save the population suffering in Zaire...If member states decide, then I will be elected and if not I will step down on December 31 this year."
